text: Performers read a script aloud as if it were evidence, then settle into arrangements borrowed from painting. Yvonne Rainer sets fiction next to documentary and declines to mark the seam: readings, fragments of dance, photographs held well past the point of recognition, tableaux vivants. Ninety minutes, and almost none of it spent on the machinery that normally fills a drama. What accumulates instead is an inspection of who is directing whom. Feeling between these people runs on something like the authority a choreographer holds over a body in a room, and the film keeps both operations in view at once, which is where its humour lives, in the joints of the arrangement rather than in any line. The National Film Registry keeps a copy of it.

One minute of film from 1896, and the entire plot is a stolen pie. William Nicholas Selig had a single short length of film, which permits exactly one idea, staged plainly enough that no title card and no English are required: a housewife's kitchen is robbed, the thief runs, the bulldog is quicker than he bargained for. The design is the interest. Comedy at the scale of a gesture, with a camera that does not move because everything funny is a matter of what crosses the frame and how fast it goes. Films this old are usually consulted rather than watched. This one still runs on the reflex it was built for, which is a stranger thing to survive well over a century than any document. The National Film Registry has it.

Eight minutes with a Black transgender woman in Los Angeles in 1967, filmed while she is living rather than while someone explains her. The date carries most of the weight. A documentary short made then, about that life, in that city, had few available forms to borrow beyond the clinical study and the exposé, and declining both is the film's argument as much as anything said in it. Nick Elliot works at the length of a visit. Eight minutes is not time enough to build a case, which suits a subject who is not a case, and the brevity reads as proportion rather than limitation. What the National Film Registry preserved is a small quantity of ordinary time: a person in her own city, at her own scale, well before there was settled public language for saying so.

Two minutes of Mardi Gras, shot in 1898 on film sixty-eight millimetres wide. That gauge is why the images still hold: a negative that size carries detail a later century can actually scan. Frederick S. Armitage set the camera where the carnival was and let the crowd supply the motion, which is the whole method available to him and, on this subject, sufficient. The physical history is half the story. An analogue preservation in 1998 produced a 35 mm duplicate negative; that duplicate was scanned in 2022 at Eye Collection Center, part of a digital pass through some two hundred surviving Mutoscope and Biograph titles. The film then turned up at the centre of an exhibition, The Artistry of REX, at the Louisiana State Museum, back in front of an audience.

A film crew in 1941 is trying to raise the money to film Chunghyang, the story every Korean already knows. That is the trap the picture is built on: the most familiar tale available is the one nobody will pay for. Lee Byung-il puts the apparatus on screen, backers and sets and schedules, and at the centre of it a director whose budget is failing and whose attention is split between two women who want incompatible things from him. Eighty-four minutes, and the pressure is arithmetical before it is artistic: sums owed, dates that cannot move, a production that stops unless someone does something unwise. Films about filmmaking usually flatter the people who make them. This one keeps the ledger open while its hero talks himself into a decision. KOFA counts it among a hundred Korean films.

The address is the film: a poor quarter of Seoul, 1982, and 108 minutes spent inside it. Bae Chang-ho treats the crowding as a set of practical facts rather than a symptom, rent and work and debt and whose turn it is to be owed a favour, and the ordinary decency these neighbours manage with one another registers as an achievement with a price on it, not as the consolation the poor are assumed to be issued instead of money. Melodrama is standing right there. The material invites it at every turn, and the steadying force is the film's patience with the business of getting through a week, its refusal to arrive from outside the gate carrying a thesis. Harmony among people with nothing is easy to film sentimentally and hard to film honestly. It sits on the KOFA hundred.

Two jewel thieves are working the same wealthy houses, and one of them is played by the man directing the picture. Francis Ford casts himself opposite Cunard and gives her the equal half of it, a rivalry between professionals, each closing on the same marks. Thirteen minutes leaves no room for motive or backstory, and none is missed. What the film runs on is procedure: approach, cover, the moment a plan has to make room for somebody else's plan. The interest is structural rather than psychological, nearer to watching two clocks than two characters, and the pace assumes an audience already fluent in the form. It is on the National Film Registry, an unusual afterlife for a crime short of 1917.

A confidence woman finishes a prison term and books herself into a Wisconsin spa hotel, which happens to belong to the husband she walked out on. She checks in as a countess. The two daughters she abandoned as infants are on the premises, and she does not tell them who she is; that withholding is the engine, and Alexander Hall runs it at seventy-two minutes, quick enough that the fraud and the family business share one clock. The National Board of Review put the picture among its ten for 1932. What holds up is the appraising eye Martha Hicks brings to the life she left: she looks at daughters, husband and hotel the way she looks at any mark, for what might be got out of them, and the film is in no hurry to correct her.

A household keeps burying its sons, and the exorcists it hires keep failing. The heir now lying in a coma is the current occasion, which is why a young woman is brought onto the property with a job to do and a line of predecessors who could not do it. Lee Doo-yong builds the fear out of position rather than apparition: she is not a visitor with a method but an employee, working inside a family compound, under the people whose affliction she has been paid to remove. Ninety-three minutes of an old house in which everyone's standing depends on an inheritance that keeps dying. What the film is anxious about is the lineage itself, a family so committed to producing male heirs that it will hire anyone and keep the arrangement quiet. It is on the KOFA hundred.

Three years after a coal-waste dam gave way above a hollow in southern West Virginia, Mimi Pickering went back with a camera and a question about ownership. The collapse killed 125 people and left 4,000 without homes; the Pittston Company called it an act of God. Forty minutes is enough for what follows, because the argument is made from dates and documents rather than rhetoric, regulations broken and hazards known in advance, set against footage of the flood itself and against survivors who describe that morning in the vocabulary of a place rather than of a case. Company officials sit for interviews too, alongside union and citizens' group representatives. The film keeps its composure while the denials keep arriving. The National Film Registry took it in.

Four people share a house called the Blue Mansion in the suburbs of Seoul, and then a fifth moves in. Se-ran keeps the place on Hyeon-ma's money; her sister Mi-ran and a maid live there with her; Hyeon-ma arrives with Dan-ju, a newly hired secretary who is also his lover. Ha Gil-jong lets the arrangement do most of the work. Eighty-nine minutes on one property, with every person's standing set by their standing with one man, and the film watches what that does to the rooms: who may enter, who waits, who is permitted to be seen. The mystery is not a crime awaiting solution but a pressure that keeps rising indoors. Made in 1972, about an attachment nobody in the house can name aloud, it says a great deal through doorways and furniture. KOFA has it among a hundred.

A phone call about a dead uncle, and a niece who happens to make documentaries. Lourdes Portillo went to Mexico to establish how Oscar died and came back with the family instead. The ruling was suicide; her relatives preferred murder, and they were generous with suspects, among them a business partner, a ranch hand, and the young widow who stands to inherit. Portillo films them all, adds snapshots and home movies, and treats gossip as a form of evidence, which is the honest move: what she can actually document is not the death but the manufacture of versions. Eighty-two minutes, and the inquiry keeps sliding into an inheritance dispute conducted in anecdote. She is not a neutral party and never claims to be. The National Film Registry holds it.

An American picture from 1939 in which nobody speaks English. Verbena trágica takes place in a Spanish-speaking New York neighbourhood on the eve of Columbus Day, with a street fiesta being got ready, and into that preparation comes Mateo, a boxer just released after a term for assault. The calendar does the work. A holiday obliges everyone to be out in the same street at the same hour, a difficult condition for a man returning with a record and a temper the block remembers. Charles Lamont directs it straight, as melodrama, with the neighbourhood as jury and the fiesta running on schedule regardless. Seventy-two minutes, and the interest lies less in what Mateo hears on his first day back than in how many people are watching him hear it. The National Film Registry has it.
